title: Platform Economics & Two-Sided Network Effects
subtitle: Why the most valuable companies of the century own no inventory — and how they win the chicken-and-egg game.

chapters.title: Simple Business Case
chapters.analogy: Think of a platform as a **night-club owner**, not a bartender. The bartender makes money selling drinks (a pipeline). The club owner makes money because people come to meet *other people*. A club with nobody in it is worthless, no matter how good the music. A packed club becomes more attractive with every new guest — and that crowd is the moat.
chapters.summary: Platforms create value by connecting two (or more) groups who need each other — buyers and sellers, riders and drivers, developers and users. Each new participant on one side makes the platform more valuable for the other side. That feedback loop is the **network effect**, and when it works, it tends to produce winner-take-most markets.

takeaways.title: The flywheel
takeaways.text: More sellers → more choice → more buyers → more revenue opportunity → more sellers.

takeaways.title: The hard part
takeaways.text: Day one has no buyers and no sellers. Solving the "chicken-and-egg" problem is the whole game.

takeaways.title: The pricing twist
takeaways.text: Platforms often subsidise one side (free for users) and monetise the other (fees for merchants).

chapters.oneLiner: A pipeline sells products. A platform sells access to each other.

chapters.title: Detailed Framework Breakdown
chapters.intro: Platform strategy flips the classical value-chain logic. Instead of controlling inputs and pushing products downstream, a platform orchestrates interactions between external producers and consumers. Value creation moves from *inside* the firm to the *ecosystem* around it. The four building blocks below are the levers every platform strategist must pull.

sections.heading: 1. Map the Sides and the Core Interaction
sections.body: Start by naming the producers, the consumers, and the single repeatable unit of value exchanged between them (a ride, a listing, a video view). Everything else — features, pricing, policies — should make that core interaction easier, more frequent, or higher quality.
bullets: **Participants:** who creates value, who consumes it, and who can switch roles (e.g., Airbnb guests becoming hosts).
**Value unit:** the atomic piece of information or product that is matched.
**Filter:** the algorithm or curation that decides which value unit reaches which consumer.

sections.heading: 2. Understand the Types of Network Effects
sections.body: Not all network effects are equal. Their direction and strength determine how defensible the platform is.
bullets: **Same-side (direct):** more users on a side attract more users on that same side (WhatsApp, LinkedIn).
**Cross-side (indirect):** more users on one side attract the other side (Uber riders ↔ drivers).
**Negative effects:** congestion, spam or competition among sellers can reduce value as the network grows — curation must scale with size.
**Local vs. global:** Uber's effects are city-local (easier to attack); Visa's are global (much harder).

sections.heading: 3. Solve the Chicken-and-Egg Problem
sections.body: Early platforms have zero value. Proven ignition tactics include:
bullets: **Single-side utility first ("come for the tool, stay for the network"):** OpenTable gave restaurants booking software before diners arrived.
**Subsidise the harder side:** Uber guaranteed hourly earnings to early drivers.
**Seed supply manually:** Reddit founders posted under fake accounts; Airbnb photographed listings themselves.
**Piggyback an existing network:** PayPal on eBay; Airbnb cross-posting to Craigslist.
**Constrain the market:** Facebook launched at one campus at a time to reach local density.

sections.heading: 4. Monetise Without Breaking the Flywheel
sections.body: Charging too early or charging the wrong side can kill the network. Monetise where willingness-to-pay is highest and price-sensitivity is lowest — typically the side that captures the most direct economic value.
bullets: **Transaction fee (take rate):** % of GMV — Airbnb, Etsy, App Store.
**Access/subscription:** charge for premium visibility or tools — LinkedIn Premium.
**Advertising:** monetise attention while keeping consumer access free — Google, Meta.
**Enhanced curation:** pay for promoted placement — Amazon Sponsored Products.

rows: Value creation | Inside the firm, linear | In the ecosystem, via interactions
Key asset | Inventory, factories, IP | Network of participants & data
Scaling cost | Grows roughly with output | Near-zero marginal cost per interaction
Competitive moat | Economies of scale (supply-side) | Network effects (demand-side)
Core metric | Units sold, margin | Liquidity, match rate, take rate, GMV
Market structure | Multiple viable players | Tends toward winner-take-most
Main risk | Cost-out competitors | Multi-homing, disintermediation, regulation
Take rate | Transactions are on-platform and high value | Leakage (users go off-platform) | Airbnb ~14–16%
Subscription | Recurring utility for producers | Slows supply acquisition | Shopify, LinkedIn
Advertising | Huge consumer attention, low WTP | Degrades user experience | Meta, YouTube
Freemium tools | One side needs SaaS workflow | Low conversion | OpenTable, Toast

chapters.title: Real-World Application
chapters.tagline: From air mattresses to a global hospitality network with ~8M listings
chapters.context: In 2008 Airbnb faced the textbook cold-start problem: travellers would not visit a site with no listings, and hosts would not list on a site with no travellers. Incumbent hotel chains owned the inventory and the brand trust. Airbnb owned neither.

execution.text: Founders flew to New York, met hosts in person and professionally photographed their homes — booking volume in the city roughly doubled after better photos.
Built a growth hack that let hosts cross-post listings to Craigslist, borrowing an existing audience to seed demand.
Introduced two-way reviews, verified IDs, secure payments held in escrow and the Host Guarantee — reducing the risk of transacting with strangers.
Expanded city-by-city, using local density as the unit of success, then layered on Experiences and long-term stays to deepen engagement.

drivers: **Trust infrastructure** turned a risky stranger-interaction into a routine purchase.
**Split fee structure** (small host fee, larger guest service fee) kept supply acquisition friction-free.
**Supply heterogeneity** — treehouses, castles, entire homes — created selection hotels could not match.
**Asset-light model** allowed rapid global expansion with minimal capital.

lessons.title: Do things that don't scale
lessons.text: Manual seeding of supply is not a failure of strategy; it is the strategy at the ignition stage.

lessons.title: Trust is a product feature
lessons.text: In two-sided markets, reducing perceived risk unlocks more transactions than lowering price.

lessons.title: Watch the negative effects
lessons.text: Over-tourism and housing-cost regulation in cities like Barcelona and New York show that platforms must manage externalities to keep their licence to operate.

chapters.title: Case Competition Slide Strategy
chapters.intro: Judges see dozens of decks. A tight three-slide spine forces you to tell one story: *why now → what we do → what it's worth*. Use this structure when the case asks you to launch, defend or grow a marketplace.

slides.title: Situation & Trigger
slides.headline: "Fragmented supply and unmet demand create a $XB matching gap"
content: Quantify both sides: # of potential producers vs. consumers
Show the friction cost today (search time, idle capacity, price opacity)
Name the trigger: tech shift, regulation, or behaviour change that makes a platform viable now
slides.visual: Two-column "supply vs demand" bar chart with the gap highlighted

slides.title: Core Solution Architecture
slides.headline: "A curated two-sided marketplace ignited city-by-city"
content: Platform canvas: producers, consumers, value unit, filter
Cold-start plan: which side you subsidise and why
Trust & quality mechanisms + monetisation model (take rate %)
slides.visual: Flywheel diagram with the ignition lever marked in accent colour

slides.title: Impact & Execution
slides.headline: "Reaching liquidity in 3 launch markets unlocks $Y revenue by Year 3"
content: Top 3 risks (multi-homing, leakage, regulation) with mitigations and KPIs
slides.visual: Stacked GMV waterfall + 3-phase Gantt strip + risk matrix

tips: Lead each slide with an action title that states the conclusion, not the topic.
Always show the metric that proves liquidity (match rate, time-to-fill, repeat rate).
Anticipate the judge's question: "What stops a competitor from copying this?" — answer with network density.

chapters.title: Inspired Startup Idea & Financials
chapters.tagline: A B2B marketplace matching retired senior engineers with SMEs for on-demand technical advisory.
chapters.name: SkillSwap Pro
chapters.problem: Small manufacturers cannot afford full-time senior engineering talent, while thousands of recently retired engineers want flexible, meaningful work. Existing freelancing platforms are generalist and lack vetting for deep industrial expertise.
chapters.solution: A curated two-sided platform with skills verification, scoped "advisory sprints" (4–20 hours), escrowed payments and outcome-based reviews. Ignition via partnerships with engineering alumni associations (supply) and regional manufacturing chambers (demand).
